items.title: Japan's debt-to-GDP is over 250% — and it hasn't defaulted
items.claim: Japan's general government gross debt was around 263% of GDP in 2023 (IMF). What's the orthodox explanation for why this hasn't triggered a sovereign debt crisis?

options.text: Japan does not actually have debt

Debt is mostly held domestically (BOJ, pension funds, banks) in yen, with the BOJ controlling the curve; net debt is lower; current account surplus; large household savings. Foreign-currency emerging market debt is structurally different

items.reveal_title: Composition matters as much as level
items.reveal:
Reinhart and Rogoff's controversial 2010 'Growth in a Time of Debt' suggested debt above 90% of GDP harmed growth. Subsequent re-analysis (Herndon, Ash, Pollin 2013) found an Excel error and weaker results. The relationship between debt levels and outcomes depends heavily on currency denomination, holders, monetary regime and growth rates.

Greece (2010-12) and Sri Lanka (2022) had foreign-currency exposure that Japan lacks. The UK has a Liability Driven Investment (LDI) crisis in autumn 2022 despite much lower debt levels — composition and confidence matter.
items.why: Headline debt-to-GDP misleads about sustainability. Currency, holders, maturity profile, monetary regime and growth trajectory matter as much as the ratio itself.

items.title: Tulip mania was less extreme than the legend
items.claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions' painted 17th-century Dutch tulip mania as a society-wide frenzy that crashed the economy. What does modern research find?

options.text: The crash bankrupted the Dutch Republic for a generation

Trading was confined largely to a small group of professional florists meeting in taverns; while bulb prices rose sharply and crashed in February 1637, the macro impact was modest and Mackay's tales of devastated cobblers are mostly unverified
Tulip mania never happened; it is a complete fabrication
It triggered the Eighty Years' War

items.reveal_title: A bubble, but a smaller one
items.reveal:
Anne Goldgar's 'Tulipmania' (2007) used archival records to show that bulb trading was largely among well-off merchants, that few contracts were ever actually enforced after the February 1637 crash, and that contemporary Calvinist moral pamphlets exaggerated the social ruin for didactic purposes.

Peter Garber argued similarly from an economist's perspective: peak prices for rare bulbs may have reflected genuine scarcity and fashion premiums, not pure delusion.

Mackay's account was readable, lurid and influential — but not historical.
items.why: Pop economic history is full of morality tales. The actual record is usually messier and less satisfying — but it's what students of bubbles need to grapple with.

items.title: Perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description
items.claim: Perfect competition (many small firms, homogeneous products, free entry, perfect information) is taught as a foundational market structure. Which is most accurate?

options.text: Most real markets fit the model closely
Real-world markets rarely satisfy the assumptions; agriculture, currency trading and some commodity markets come closer than most. The model is useful as a normative benchmark, not as descriptive
Perfect competition is identical to monopoly
No real-world market resembles it at all

items.reveal:
Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin 1933) and game-theoretic oligopoly models (Cournot 1838, Bertrand 1883, Stackelberg 1934) capture more of the realistic market structures.

Key deviations: most product markets have differentiated products; information is imperfect (Akerlof's 'lemons' 1970); entry has costs; small numbers of dominant firms common. The 'IO revolution' from the 1970s onwards (Tirole's textbook, 1988) built strategic-interaction-based frameworks.
items.why: The perfect competition model serves as a welfare benchmark in policy analysis. Treating it as a description of how markets work misses what most of industrial economics has been building toward.
